claims.text: Six hours of high-energy ball milling generates sufficient lattice strain and grain refinement in equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi.
Milling-induced lattice strain and grain refinement lower the thermodynamic energy barrier for a metastable FCC-to-BCC solid-solution transition.
SPS at 1000°C after six hours of milling enables a single-phase BCC CoCrFeNiTi structure.
The VEC and atomic-radius mismatch of CoCrFeNiTi suppress brittle HCP Ti-rich precipitation at 1000°C.
The equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi powder has a metastable FCC solid-solution tendency because of high configurational entropy.
CoCrFeNiTi is prone to HCP precipitation during thermal processing.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi has a target VEC of approximately 7.5.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNiTi has an atomic-radius mismatch greater than 4.5%.
Severe plastic deformation during milling produces high-density dislocation networks and nanocrystalline grain boundaries.
Milling-generated dislocations and grain boundaries act as nucleation sites for the BCC phase.
The milling-generated defects inhibit HCP nucleation by reducing the critical radius for phase transformation.
Milling-induced strain energy together with the CoCrFeNiTi VEC shifts the Gibbs free-energy minimum toward BCC.
SPS at 1000°C provides enough thermal activation for densification and phase ordering without crossing the kinetic threshold for Ti-driven HCP precipitation.
Suppressed diffusion in the nanocrystalline state helps prevent Ti-driven HCP precipitation.
The proposed process will produce a greater-than-98%-dense alloy with negligible porosity.
The resulting microstructure will be single-phase BCC or BCC+B2 with no detectable HCP phase.
The processed alloy will have higher Vickers hardness than cast CoCrFeNiTi because of grain-boundary and solid-solution strengthening.
Conventionally arc-melted CoCrFeNiTi typically has an FCC+BCC or multiphase structure, significant porosity, and lower hardness associated with coarse grains and possible HCP precipitation.
Above 1050°C, rapid grain growth and thermodynamic precipitation of HCP Ti-rich phases occur and degrade mechanical properties.
Vickers testing at a 100 g load minimizes indentation-size effects and isolates grain-boundary strengthening from precipitation hardening.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts a single-phase BCC structure, whereas the predicted outcome allows either single-phase BCC or a BCC+B2 microstructure.

The boundary states that decomposition and grain growth occur only when temperature exceeds 1050°C, but the experiment uses exactly 1050°C as the high-temperature control and treats failure to observe increased HCP precipitation there as evidence that the boundary is wrong.
